subject: science
passage: Kea, large parrots of New Zealand's mountains, often engage in rough play, chasing, wrestling, and tossing one another, and a particular warbling call is commonly heard during these bouts. Researchers have found that hearing a recording of this call can prompt kea to start playing. Behavioral ecologist Hemi Walker suspects that the call does more than spread a playful mood. He hypothesizes that it also tells other birds that the pecking and grappling that follow are not real aggression, which reduces the chance that a play bout turns into a genuine fight.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Walker's hypothesis?

choices.A: Play bouts that began without the warbling call turned into real fights more often than bouts that began with it.
choices.B: Kea that heard a recording of the warbling call began playing even when no other kea were anywhere nearby to play with.
choices.C: Real fights broke out after play bouts as often when the warbling call had been given as when it had not.
choices.D: Young kea give the warbling call more often than adult kea do, and they also play more often.

explanation.why: Walker's hypothesis goes beyond the known finding that the call spreads play: he claims the call marks rough behavior as harmless and so prevents fights. Support must connect the call to fewer fights. A comparison showing that bouts without the call escalate into fights more often does this directly.
explanation.A: Correct. Bouts that lacked the call were more likely to become real fights, which fits the idea that the call signals that the rough behavior is play.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This shows only that the call puts kea in a mood to play, the earlier finding Walker says is not the whole story; it says nothing about preventing fights.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If the call made no difference to how often fights broke out, the hypothesis would be weakened.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Who calls and plays most often does not show whether the call keeps play from becoming aggression.
